Lesson 15 / Part 1: Don't lose my work / ~35 minutes

Being Asked First

Three stages, your first hand-written enum, and the end of part 1.

Lesson 13 taught the editor to know when a buffer has unsaved edits. Lesson 14 gave you a way to close a buffer. Put those together and you have an editor that knows perfectly well it's about to throw your work away, and does it anyway.

This lesson makes it ask. It's the last of part 1, and at the end of it the bug that opened lesson 13 — close the window, lose the afternoon — is gone by every route.

A destructive action that can't be stopped isn't a feature, it's a trap.
The fix is not a warning. It's a question, asked before anything happens.

Where you're starting

Lesson 14's editor, with closable tabs. Check against lesson 14's checkpoint.

Ask before closing

Closing a modified buffer puts a question on screen instead.

The close path already knows everything it needs — closing holds the index and buffer.dirty says whether it matters. What's missing is somewhere to park the request while the question is on screen. Five edits.

First — the parking space:

editor/src/main.rsthe Editor struct

struct Editor {
    buffers: Vec<Buffer>,
    active: usize,
    /// A buffer whose closing is held up until the question on screen is answered.
    confirm: Option<usize>,
    position: String,

Second — nothing is pending when the editor starts:

editor/src/main.rsin Editor::open

            active: 0,
            confirm: None,
            position: "no cursor".to_owned(),

Third — closing now branches on whether there's anything to lose:

editor/src/main.rsin fn ui, where closing is applied

            if let Some(index) = closing {
                self.close(index);
                if self.buffers[index].dirty {
                    self.confirm = Some(index);
                } else {
                    self.close(index);
                }
            }

A clean buffer still closes instantly. Asking about something with nothing to lose is how confirmation dialogs train people to click through them without reading — the question is only worth asking when the answer could differ.

Fourth — the question itself, as a new impl Editor block just above impl eframe::App for Editor:

editor/src/main.rsabove impl eframe::App for Editor

impl Editor {
    /// Draw the question, and act on the answer.
    fn ask(&mut self, ui: &egui::Ui, index: usize) {
        let question = format!("{} has unsaved changes.", self.buffers[index].name());

        egui::Modal::new(egui::Id::new("confirm")).show(ui.ctx(), |ui| {
            ui.heading("Unsaved changes");
            ui.label(question);
            ui.add_space(8.0);

            ui.horizontal(|ui| {
                if ui.button("Discard").clicked() {
                    self.confirm = None;
                    self.close(index);
                }
                if ui.button("Cancel").clicked() {
                    self.confirm = None;
                }
            });
        });
    }
}

What a modal is, and why it takes a Context

egui::Modal is a centred window with a backdrop that swallows clicks aimed at anything behind it. That backdrop is the whole point: while the question is up, the tab bar and the text box are still drawn, but nothing you click on them reaches them.

Notice it takes ui.ctx() rather than ui. Everything you've drawn so far has gone into a panel — a region with a position in a layout. A modal doesn't belong to any region; it floats above all of them, so it's addressed to the context, the thing that owns the whole frame. That's also why it can be called from the end of fn ui, after every panel has closed.

Why question is built before the closure format!("{} has unsaved changes.", self.buffers[index].name()) borrows self. The closure below it needs &mut self to call self.close(index). Building the string first, into a String the closure owns, ends that borrow before the closure starts — otherwise this is E0502, a borrow of self.buffers still alive while self is borrowed mutably.

        if let Some(index) = self.confirm {

        self.frame_ms = frame_start.elapsed().as_secs_f32() * 1000.0;

Ask before quitting too

The window's close button stops being fatal.

Closing a tab now asks. Closing the window still doesn't — and that's the route that started lesson 13, where the whole afternoon went. It's also the route where Option<usize> stops being enough: there's no index to put in it. Quitting isn't about a buffer.

You need a type that says "one of these two things", and Rust's word for that is enum. You've used two of them constantly — Option and Result — without writing one. Eight edits, and the file won't compile until they're all in.

First — the type, just above struct Buffer:

editor/src/main.rsabove the Buffer struct

/// Something the editor is waiting for permission to do.
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
enum Pending {
    Close(usize),
    Quit,
}

An enum is a choice, and it can carry luggage

A Pending is either a Close — which carries a usize, the buffer it means — or a Quit, which carries nothing because there's nothing to say. Not both, never neither.

That's the same shape as the enums you already use. Option::Some carries a value and None doesn't; Result::Ok and Err each carry something different. Rust's enums are not C's numbered constants — each variant is its own little struct, and the compiler makes you say which one you have before you can reach inside.

#[derive(Clone, Copy)] is what lets you write if let Some(pending) = self.confirm and get a copy rather than a borrow. Without it that line would borrow self.confirm, and the borrow would still be alive when the closure below tried to set it — E0502 again. A Copy enum this small is two machine words; copying it is cheaper than reasoning about who borrowed it.

Second — the field changes type:

editor/src/main.rsthe Editor struct

    confirm: Option<usize>,
    /// An action held up until the question on screen is answered.

Fourth — quitting needs to know whether anything is at stake, which is a count:

editor/src/main.rsin impl Editor, above fn close

    /// How many buffers hold edits that aren't on disk?
    fn unsaved(&self) -> usize {
        self.buffers.iter().filter(|buffer| buffer.dirty).count()
    }

Fifth — the question now has two forms:

editor/src/main.rsin fn ask, the top

    /// Draw the question, and act on the answer.
    fn ask(&mut self, ui: &egui::Ui, index: usize) {
        let question = format!("{} has unsaved changes.", self.buffers[index].name());
    fn ask(&mut self, ui: &egui::Ui, pending: Pending) {
        let question = match pending {
            Pending::Close(index) => format!("{} has unsaved changes.", self.buffers[index].name()),
            Pending::Quit => format!("{} file(s) have unsaved changes.", self.unsaved()),
        };

That match is exhaustive, and the compiler checks it. Add a third variant to Pending later — say CloseAll — and every match on it becomes an error until you've said what the new case does. That is the property that makes enums worth reaching for.

Sixth — Discard stops knowing what it's discarding, and defers to a method that does:

editor/src/main.rsin impl Editor, after fn ask

    /// Do the thing that was waiting on an answer.
    fn carry_out(&mut self, pending: Pending, ui: &egui::Ui) {
        self.confirm = None;
        match pending {
            Pending::Close(index) => self.close(index),
            Pending::Quit => ui.ctx().send_viewport_cmd(egui::ViewportCommand::Close),

Eighth — and the quit itself, replacing the block you added in stage 1:

editor/src/main.rsin fn ui, just above the frame timer

        if let Some(index) = self.confirm {

        if ui.input(|i| i.viewport().close_requested()) && self.unsaved() > 0 {
            ui.ctx()
                .send_viewport_cmd(egui::ViewportCommand::CancelClose);
            self.confirm = Some(Pending::Quit);

        if let Some(pending) = self.confirm {
            self.ask(ui, pending);

Cancelling a close that has already happened

The window manager doesn't ask permission — it tells you. By the time close_requested() is true, the decision has been made and egui will shut the application down at the end of this frame unless you say otherwise.

ViewportCommand::CancelClose is saying otherwise. It's not "please don't close"; it's "revoke the close that's already in flight". Send it, park a Pending::Quit, and the window stays up with a question on it. When the answer comes, carry_out sends ViewportCommand::Close — which this time nothing revokes.

cargo run -- a.rs b.rs
→ type into a tab, then click the window's close button
→ the window stays, and asks
→ Cancel keeps working; Discard quits
→ with nothing modified, the close button just closes

I checked this one without a window close_requested() is self.events.contains(&ViewportEvent::Close) and that events vector is public, so the whole quit path can be driven headlessly by pushing the event in. All four cases above were run that way before this lesson was written — including that a click on Discard really does take the buffer count from 2 to 1.

Offer to save, not just to lose

A third button that does the obvious thing.

Right now the question has two answers, and both of them are bad: throw the work away, or don't do the thing you asked for. The answer anyone actually wants is "save it, then carry on". Three edits.

First — the button, ahead of the other two:

editor/src/main.rsin fn ask, the button row

            ui.horizontal(|ui| {
                if ui.button("Save").clicked() {
                    self.save_for(pending);
                    self.carry_out(pending, ui);
                }
                if ui.button("Discard").clicked() {

Save is first because it's the answer that loses nothing. In a dialog about destroying work, the safe option should be the one your hand is already on.

Second — what it calls:

editor/src/main.rsin impl Editor, above fn carry_out

    /// Write out whatever the pending action is about to throw away.
    fn save_for(&mut self, pending: Pending) {
        let indices: Vec<usize> = match pending {
            Pending::Close(index) => vec![index],
            Pending::Quit => (0..self.buffers.len())
                .filter(|index| self.buffers[*index].dirty)
                .collect(),
        };

        for index in indices {
            if let Err(error) = self.buffers[index].save() {
                self.buffers[index].status = format!("save failed: {error}");
            }
        }
    }

Why the indices are collected first

The obvious version of that function iterates the buffers and saves the dirty ones in one pass. It doesn't compile: iterating self.buffers borrows it, and buffer.save() needs &mut — you'd be reading and writing the same vector at once.

Collecting the indices first ends the read before the writes start. That's the same move as lesson 14's closing variable: decide while you're reading, act once you've stopped. The difference is instructive — in lesson 14 the compiler let the bad version through and it panicked at run time, because indices aren't borrows. Here the values are borrows, so it's a compile error instead.

Third — three tests, at the bottom of mod tests:

editor/src/main.rsin mod tests, at the end

    #[test]
    fn a_fresh_editor_has_nothing_unsaved() {
        assert_eq!(editor_with(&["a.rs", "b.rs"]).unsaved(), 0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn unsaved_counts_every_modified_buffer() {
        let mut editor = editor_with(&["a.rs", "b.rs", "c.rs"]);
        editor.buffers[0].dirty = true;
        editor.buffers[2].dirty = true;
        assert_eq!(editor.unsaved(), 2);
    }

    #[test]
    fn closing_a_buffer_forgets_its_unsaved_edits() {
        let mut editor = editor_with(&["a.rs", "b.rs"]);
        editor.buffers[0].dirty = true;
        editor.close(0);
        assert_eq!(editor.unsaved(), 0);
    }
}

Where you ended up

613 lines, seventeen tests green. One new type, and one new impl Editor block holding the question and its consequences.

editor/src/main.rsthe confirmation, above impl eframe::App

impl Editor {
    /// Draw the question, and act on the answer.
    fn ask(&mut self, ui: &egui::Ui, pending: Pending) {
        let question = match pending {
            Pending::Close(index) => format!("{} has unsaved changes.", self.buffers[index].name()),
            Pending::Quit => format!("{} file(s) have unsaved changes.", self.unsaved()),
        };

        egui::Modal::new(egui::Id::new("confirm")).show(ui.ctx(), |ui| {
            ui.heading("Unsaved changes");
            ui.label(question);
            ui.add_space(8.0);

            ui.horizontal(|ui| {
                if ui.button("Save").clicked() {
                    self.save_for(pending);
                    self.carry_out(pending, ui);
                }
                if ui.button("Discard").clicked() {
                    self.carry_out(pending, ui);
                }
                if ui.button("Cancel").clicked() {
                    self.confirm = None;
                }
            });
        });
    }

    /// Write out whatever the pending action is about to throw away.
    fn save_for(&mut self, pending: Pending) {
        let indices: Vec<usize> = match pending {
            Pending::Close(index) => vec![index],
            Pending::Quit => (0..self.buffers.len())
                .filter(|index| self.buffers[*index].dirty)
                .collect(),
        };

        for index in indices {
            if let Err(error) = self.buffers[index].save() {
                self.buffers[index].status = format!("save failed: {error}");
            }
        }
    }

    /// Do the thing that was waiting on an answer.
    fn carry_out(&mut self, pending: Pending, ui: &egui::Ui) {
        self.confirm = None;
        match pending {
            Pending::Close(index) => self.close(index),
            Pending::Quit => ui.ctx().send_viewport_cmd(egui::ViewportCommand::Close),
        }
    }
}
The rest is as lesson 14 left it Pending sits above struct Buffer; Editor gained a confirm field and an unsaved method; fn ui gained the quit check and the call to ask. Everything else — Text, Buffer, the scanner, the panels — is unchanged.

Check yourself

Why did Option<usize> stop being enough in stage 2?

  • Quitting isn't about any particular buffer
  • An index can't be copied out of an Option
  • Two confirmations can be pending at once
  • usize can't represent "no buffer selected"

The pending action became one of two shapes — close this buffer, or quit, which carries nothing. An enum says "one of these", and each variant carries exactly the luggage its case needs. ↑ Review: an enum is a choice (stage 2)

What does ViewportCommand::CancelClose actually do?

  • Revokes a close that is already in flight
  • Asks the window manager for permission to stay open
  • Suppresses the close button until it is re-enabled
  • Delays the close until the next frame

By the time close_requested() is true the decision is made and egui will shut down at the end of the frame. CancelClose takes it back; without it, your question would appear for one frame and then vanish with the window. ↑ Review: cancelling a close (stage 2)

Why is question built before the modal's closure rather than inside it?

  • It ends a borrow of self before the closure needs &mut self
  • Formatting inside a closure allocates on every frame
  • The closure runs before the surrounding function body
  • Modal::show requires its content to be pre-computed

Reading self.buffers[index].name() borrows self. The closure calls self.close(index), which needs a mutable borrow. Producing an owned String first ends the first borrow before the second begins. ↑ Review: why question is built first (stage 1)

Why does save_for collect indices before saving anything?

  • Iterating the buffers borrows what save must mutate
  • Saving reorders the buffers, invalidating the iterator
  • Collecting lets the saves run in parallel
  • A Vec cannot be iterated twice in one function

You'd be reading the vector and writing to its elements at once. Collecting ends the read first — the same "decide while reading, act after" move as lesson 14, except here the compiler rejects the bad version instead of letting it panic. ↑ Review: why the indices are collected (stage 3)

Part 1 is finished

Three lessons ago the editor would silently eat an afternoon's work. It now knows what you've changed, shows you on the tab, refuses to close a buffer or the window without asking, and offers to save when you say yes. The bug that opened lesson 13 is closed by every route into it.

What you picked up on the way, in Rust terms: change detection against a cheap snapshot, the borrow rules around closures that mutate what they read, deferred mutation as a pattern, index arithmetic that a test caught before you did, and your own enum with data in its variants.

Primary source: The Rust Programming Language, Chapter 6 — Enums and Pattern Matching. You've now written one, so the chapter will read as confirmation rather than introduction — which is the right order. 6.2 on match and 6.3 on if let are the ones worth slowing down for, because you've been using both since lesson 2 without ever seeing them defined.

I'm your teacher here — ask me things. The weakest part of this lesson is the quit dialog: it says "2 file(s) have unsaved changes" and gives you one Save button for all of them. A real editor lists the files and lets you choose per file, and the reason this one doesn't is that it would double the lesson. If that bothers you, it's a good thing to build unprompted — you have every piece already.
